The accused were charged with the wilful promotion of hatred contrary to s.
281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
as a result of their involvement in the
publication and distribution of a publication known as the Nationalist Reporter
and other material distributed by the Nationalist Party of Canada of which they
were members. This literature advanced the theory of white supremacy and
identified as inferior "non-whites and non- Aryan groups" which were
portrayed as intellectually inferior and unclean. The trial judge convicted the
accused of the offence although he accepted that the accused were expressing a
sincerely held belief. On appeal from their conviction the accused argued that
s. 281.2(2) of the Criminal Code was unconstitutional.

Held, the appeal against conviction should be dismissed.

Per Grange J.A., Krever J.A. concurring: Section 281.2(2) of the
Criminal
Code
does not infringe the guarantee to freedom of expression in
s. 2(b)
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The guarantee to freedom of expression
in
s. 2(b)
was never intended to and does not give constitutional protection to
hate-mongering such as that of the accused. Freedom of expression is not
absolute and the wilful promotion of hatred is entirely antithetical to our
system of freedoms. That such conduct was not intended to be covered by the
guarantee to freedom of expression is reinforced by reference to
s. 27
of the
Charter which requires that the Charter is to be interpreted in "a manner
consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage
of Canadians". Even accepting that the accused had a sincere belief concerning
the views expressed in the material this did not minimize the offence. Indeed,
it made it more dangerous if not more heinous. In any event, even if there is
an infringement of s. 2(b) of the Charter then s. 281.2(2) constitutes a
reasonable limit within the meaning of
s. 1
of the Charter.

Further, s. 281.2 is not unconstitutional because the accused is required to
establish the defence of truth of the statements on a balance of probabilities
pursuant to s. 281.2(3)(a). Section 281.2(3)(a) does not create a true reverse
onus. The offence remains that of wilful promotion of hatred but the
Criminal
Code
provides that a defence can be raised even though the accused without that
defence would be guilty of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt. Extension of
that defence to an accused cannot be read as limiting the rights of the
accused.

Per Cory J.A.: Freedom of expression is of vital and fundamental importance
to a free and democratic society and to its citizens and a statement should
have the protection of
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

unless it was known to be false by the maker and was likely to cause injury, or
it falls within what must be the very narrow confines of the regulated area
because it is clearly antithetical to the freedom conferred by
s. 2(b)
. In this
case, the trial judge found that the accused were expressing a sincerely held
belief. Although that belief was utterly erroneous and expressed in the vilest
of terms, it was none the less an expression of a sincerely held belief and as
such it should not be held to come within the regulated area. However, s.
281.2(2) is a reasonable limit upon freedom of expression guaranteed by
s.
2
(b). Section 281.2(2) is narrowly drawn being aimed at restricting public
statements which wilfully promote hatred against a group which can be
identified by its colour, race, religion or ethnic origin. It does not in any
way restrict criticism including intemperate criticism of public institutions.
Rather, it is designed to prevent the destruction of our multicultural society,
a value confirmed in
s. 27
of the Charter itself. Further, an expression must
go a long way before it qualifies as promotion of hatred within the meaning of
s. 281.2(2). To promote hatred is to instill detestation, enmity, ill-will and
malevolence in another. When an expression does instill detestation it does
incalculable damage to the Canadian community and lays the foundation for the
mistreatment of members of the victimized group. The section was carefully
drawn to restrain freedom of expression as little as possible. The
international commitments of Canada such as signing the International
Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, and the
similar legislation enacted by other nations demonstrate that the provisions of
s. 281.2(2) are consistent with freedom and democracy. The object of s.
281.2(2) to protect identifiable groups from the wilful promotion of hatred
against them constitutes a measure of sufficient importance to warrant
overriding the constitutionally protected freedom of expression. The objective
clearly relates to a concern which is pressing and substantial. The means
chosen are proportional to that objective. They are rationally connected to the
objective and impair as little as possible the freedom of expression. The
section is limited in its application, it does not apply to statements
communicated in private conversation, does not in any way inhibit the most free
and intemperate criticism of public institutions or policies or public concern
and requires proof of wilful promotion of hatred. As well, the section creates
a number of specific defences. Finally, it is no ground for not applying
s. 1

that s. 281.2 permits the conviction of a person who causes no serious harm or
risk of harm. The risk of harm occasioned to identifiable groups by the
promotion of hatred is well established. The empirical data supporting that
conclusion established the need to restrain promotion of hatred and fully
justify the application of s. 1. Section 281.2(2) is not simply paternalistic,
well-intentioned meddling by Parliament but based upon hard, chilling facts of
history.

Criminal Law -- Sentence -- Wilful promotion of hatred -- Accused members of
white supremacist group responsible for distribution of white supremacist
material -- Following conviction accused released on bail pending appeal and
having refrained from publication of such material for a considerable period of
time -- In circumstances sentences of one year and seven months imprisonment
should be reduced on appeal to three months and one month imprisonment --
Accused also placed on probation for three years with term requiring that not
publish similar material -- Cr. Code, s. 281.2.

APPEAL by the accused from their conviction and sentence on a charge of
wilfully promoting hatred contrary to s. 281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
.

CORY J.A.:-- There are two issues that are raised on this appeal. Firstly,
is s. 281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
an infringement of that freedom of
expression which is guaranteed under
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
? Secondly, if the section is found to be an infringement of
s.
2(b)
, can it be upheld under
s. 1
of the Charter as a reasonable limit
prescribed by law and demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society?

1
. Factual background

Both of the appellants are members of the Nationalist Party of Canada, which
is described in their factum as a "white nationalist political
organization". Smith was the party secretary and Andrews was the party
leader. Both appellants were members of the party's central committee, the body
responsible for publishing and distributing the bimonthly publication of the
Nationalist Reporter together with certain other party material which form the
subject-matter of the complaint in this case.

Among the material seized pursuant to a search warrant were copies of the
Nationalist Reporter, some of which had been pre- addressed for mailing
purposes; letters to the Nationalist Reporter written by subscribers;
subscription lists; and a number of printed mimeographed sticker cards
containing messages such as "Nigger go home", "Hoax on the
Holocaust", "Israel stinks", "Hitler was right. Communism
is Jewish".

Literature published and distributed by the Nationalist Party advanced the
theory of white supremacy. It identified as inferior "non-whites and
non-Aryan groups" which were portrayed as intellectually inferior and
unclean. They were described as having a propensity to commit violent crime and
as posing an economic threat to white communities through their reliance on
social support. The material is rubbish and offal. Some excerpts will serve to
show the malodorous, malicious and evil nature of the writings.

Excerpts promoting the purity of the white race

For all men, the truth remains, and no law,
slogan, utopia, or System government will ever close that vast and natural gap
between the Whiteman and other races.

In creating man, God has taken his greatest gifts
and bestowed only a portion of us with them -- the White people. If it were
part of His plan to create one, coffee-coloured race of "humanity",
certainly one would have been created right from Genisis [sic].

Surely if God or nature had intended one
coffee-coloured race to inhabit this planet, it would have been so, ... all
those who push for a homogenous race-mixed planet are only working against
God's and nature's original will ...

Excerpts portraying members of racial minorities
as responsible for increases in the rate of violent crime

... Toronto's violent crime rate is increasing --
almost directly in proportion to the increase in immigrants from the Caribbean,
India, Pakistan and blacks from the U.S.

There has not only been an unprecedented number
of attacks, rapes and killings of women, but evidence indicates that a high proportion
of them are being committed by blacks.

Excerpts pertaining to immigration and repatriation

... [T]oday, a vast majority of the 800,000 legal
immigrants who enter America are non-white. Almost all of the illegal aliens
and refugees who come here are also coloured. AMERICA IS BEING SWAMPED BY
COLOUREDS WHO DO NOT BELIEVE IN DEMOCRACY AND HARBOUR A HATRED FOR WHITE
PEOPLE!

White Nationalists have long held that the only
way to a lasting and permanent end to our hemisphere's racial strife is the separation
of the races through repatriation of non- whites to their own lands where their
own race is the majority ...

Excerpts pertaining to Jewish persons

A letter to the editor states:

"The NPC (Nationalist Party of Canada) is
the only effective political party in Canada which can ... stop the
International Jewish Communist conspiracy."

Articles entitled "James Keegstra's fight
for truth", "Zionist Hate Compaign" and "Zionists
responsible for massacre" appear in issues of the Nationalist Reporter.
One article, referring to the holocaust as one of the Zionists' "biggest
lies", goes on to state:

"The Holocaust Hoax has been so ingrained in
the minds of the hated 'goyim' by now that in some countries, ... challenging
its validity can land you in jail."

In an article entitled "Jews no strangers to
organized crime" there is reference to ''the contribution -- and a large
one it is -- that Jews have made to the underworld". An article entitled
"Zionist Economic Power Growing" contains the following passage:

"A nation which allows a small alien
community to dominate its financial life and its resources cannot expect to
remain in good health, especially when that alien community's interests happen
to be not those of the majority of the citizens, culturally and
economically."

The Nationalist Reporter fortunately had a very low circulation. The
subscription lists indicated there were only some 43 individuals and 50 groups,
clubs or organizations which subscribed to the publication. Although it was
printed for at least three years the paper seems to have had a very small
impact despite its boastful reporting that "[i]n recent weeks over 4,000
pieces of White Nationalist literature along with White Nationalist stickers
have been distributed".

2
. Decision at trial

The appellants did not raise any issue at trial with respect to the
constitutional validity of s. 281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
.

The trial judge found the accused guilty as charged. He held that hatred
went farther than such emotions as prejudice, mere dislike, ridicule or
contempt and adopted the definition that was used in the charge to the jury in
R. v. Keegstra (1984),
1984 CanLII 1313 (AB KB)
, 19 C.C.C. (3d) 254 (Alta. Q.B.). There, hatred was
defined as "an emotion of extreme dislike or aversion, detestation,
abhorrence". He determined that wilfulness or conscious purpose or intent
are qualities of the mind that are rarely, though sometimes, proved by direct
statements of intention. Rather, he found that they were to be determined upon
a fair reading of the material itself. He decided that a fair reading of the
materials indicated that the appellants had promoted hatred against Jews and
minority groups and that this was "blatantly apparent". He stated:

In fact, those parts of the materials which deal
with the promotion of hatred against the Jews so clearly constitute the
definition of hatred that the only adjective I can think of to indicate the
degree of hatred is "obscene".

3. Does s. 281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
infringe

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter of Rights
?

Section 281.2(2) of the
Criminal Code
provides that:

281.2(2) Everyone who, by communicating
statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred
against any identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an indictable offence and is liable to
imprisonment for two years; or

(b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.

Section 281.2(3) sets out a number of defences to a charge laid under s.
281.2(2).

281.2(3) No person shall be convicted of an
offence under subsection (2)

(a) if he establishes that the statements
communicated were true;

(b) if, in good faith, he expressed or attempted to
establish by argument an opinion upon a religious subject;

(c) if the statements were relevant to any subject
of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public benefit, and if
on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true; or

(d) if, in good faith, he intended to point out,
for the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to produce feelings of
hatred towards an identifiable group in Canada.

Section 281.2(7) sets out definitions for a number of terms used in this
section.

281.2(7) In this section

"communicating" includes communicating
by telephone, broadcasting or other audible or visible means;

"identifiable group" has the same
meaning as it has in section 281.1;

"public place" includes any place to
which the public have access as of right or by invitation, express or implied;

"statements" includes words spoken or
written or recorded electronically or electromagnetically or otherwise, and
gestures, signs or other visible representations.

Section 2(b)
of the
Charter
guarantees freedom of expression in these words:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

. . . . .

(b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and
expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication;

(a) The importance of freedom of expression

Freedom of thought is of limited value without the freedom to express that
thought, to advocate the adoption of a new concept or the termination of an
institution that has become outmoded or unfair. The exchange of ideas is vital
to a democratic form of government and to its citizens. Without it democracy
simply cannot survive.

The importance of the concept was eloquently expressed in Retail, Wholesale
& Department Store Union, Local 580 v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd. (1986),
1986 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, 33
D.L.R. (4th) 174, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573, [1987] 1 W.W.R. 577 (S.C.C.), where Mr.
Justice McIntyre stated at p. 183 D.L.R., p. 583 S.C.R., that freedom of
expression:

... is one of the fundamental concepts that has
formed the basis for the historical development of the political, social and
educational institutions of western society. Representative democracy, as we
know it today, which is in great part the product of free expression and
discussion of varying ideas, depends upon its maintenance and protection.

The importance of this freedom was also stressed by this court in R. v.
Kopyto (1987),
1987 CanLII 176 (ON CA)
, 62 O.R. (2d) 449 at pp. 462-3, 39 C.C.C. (3d) 1 at p. 15, 47
D.L.R. (4th) 213. That freedom should not be readily restrained.

Statements will often be made about identifiable groups within our society
that will be contentious, irritating and annoying for they may not always be
politely phrased. Yet they should receive the protection accorded by
s. 2
(b).
No doubt when Galileo expressed his opinion that the earth revolved around the
sun he offended the church doctrine of the day and all the members of the
church, who would constitute a clearly identifiable group. Undoubtedly, that
group was outraged and shocked. History makes it clear that Galileo's treatise
engendered the enmity of the church authorities who instituted severely
restrictive measures against him. Further, the statements of Darwin as to the
origin of the species created a situation rife with conflicts which engendered
enmity between identifiable groups: the fundamentalist religions on one side
and on the other, those who espoused and supported the position of Darwin as to
the origin of human beings. The protection provided for freedom of expression
must be wide enough to permit persons to set forward new and different ideas no
matter how upsetting those ideas may be to identifiable groups.

The enactment of s. 281.2(2) of the Code arose from the "Report of the
Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada" (1966), chaired by Dean
Cohen. The committee observed that recent history had shown that individual
rights cannot be supported in absolute terms. It noted that Canadians who are
members of any identifiable group should be entitled to carry on their lives
without being victimized by the deliberate, vicious promotion of hatred against
them. The committee concluded that hate propaganda had, at that time, reached
such a stage that legislation was required. None the less, the committee
emphasized the importance of freedom of expression. It observed that freedom of
expression is a cornerstone of our way of life and that there is a strong
presumption that putting limits on it weakens our way of life. It determined
that priority had to be given to freedom of expression in making choices as to
the extent of restraint when it came to imposing restraints upon that right.
The committee put it in this way (at pp. 60-1):

Priority to Freedom of Expression. Because of
these wide borderline areas where vigorous rough and tumble debate shifts into
the brutal, the vicious and the illicit, the general preferences with which one
approaches the task of balancing interests is of crucial importance.

. . . . .

It is our opinion that the Canadian people
already have made the decision that as among conflicting values, preference
must always be given to freedom of expression rather than to legal prohibitions
directed at abuses of it. This is not to say that freedom of expression is
regarded as an absolute, but only to insist that it will be esteemed more
highly and weighted more significantly in the legislative scales, so that legal
markings of the borderline areas will always be such as to permit liberty even
at the cost of occasional license. But at some point that liberty becomes
licence and colours the quality of liberty itself with an unacceptable stain.
At that point the social preference must move from freedom to regulation to
preserve the very system of freedom itself.

The original report of the Cohen Committee recognized that the provisions of
s. 281.2 of the Code would to a limited extent infringe freedom of expression
but that these modest restraints were necessary and justifiable in the
multicultured society of Canada.

This, too, is the position taken by the Law Reform Commission of Canada,
which has recently reviewed the provisions of s. 281.2. In Working Paper No. 50
(1986), it recognized that the offence of promoting hatred is the most
problematic of all crimes. Despite this, the commission determined that the
offence should remain (at p. 39):

Admittedly, the very existence of these crimes of
fomenting hatred is open to two fundamental objections. First, they encroach
upon freedom of expression in an unjustifiable manner. In other words,
restricting freedom of expression for some restricts freedom of expression for
all. Second, they may not do what they are expected to do. After all, the
Weimar Republic had crimes of hate propaganda; yet Hitler still came to power.

The crimes proposed in this Paper, however,
infringe upon freedom of expression in a justifiable manner by ensuring that
only the most serious kinds of hatred are caught by the criminal law. Moreover,
these crimes will do what they are expected to do, in two ways: first, by
underlining the fundamental values of equality and dignity; second, by
deterring others from engaging in such activity.

(Emphasis added.)

It is significant that after careful consideration the only amendment that
the Law Reform Commission suggested to s. 281.2 is that the word
"foment" be substituted for the word "promote".

Thus, both the Cohen Commission before the passage of the legislation and
the Law Reform Commission after recently reviewing the legislation took the
position that the section interferes with the right of freedom of expression.
Before determining whether the jurisprudence in Ontario supports such a
conclusion it may be helpful first to review the position taken in the United
States with respect to the scope of the constitutional protection of free
speech, and to consider the approaches to
ss. 2
(b) and
1
that have been taken
in other Canadian provinces.

(b) Protected freedom of expression in the United
States

At the outset it should be remembered that the Constitution of the United
States does not contain a provision such as s. 1 of our
Charter
. In Beauharnais
v. Illinois, 343 U.S. 250 (1952), the United States Supreme Court by a
five-four majority upheld the conviction of a person under a provision of the
Illinois Criminal Code which provided that it was a crime to exhibit in any
public place a publication which "portrays depravity, criminality,
unchastity or lack of virtue of a class of citizens of any race, color, creed
or religion" when it "exposes the citizens of any race, color, creed
or religion to contempt, derision or obloquy or which is productive of breach
of the peace or riots". Beauharnais had accused blacks of being rapists,
robbers, knife and gun carriers, marijuana smokers and mongrelizers of the
white race. The majority of the court held that these libelous statements did
not fall within the realm of constitutionally protected free speech. In
Garrison v. Louisiana, 379 U.S. 64 (1964), the Supreme Court appeared to modify
its position and found that some libelous statements that were caught by state
criminal libel statutes did indeed come within the realm of constitutionally
protected free speech. As a result of the decision some American writers
considered that the Beauharnais decision had been placed in serious doubt. E.T.
Marcus, "Group Defamation and Individual Actions: A New Look at an Old
Rule" (1983), 71 Cal. L. Rev. 1532 at p. 1547:

... [C]riminal defamation laws are virtually
non-existent in modern criminal codes. But even if such statutes exist and are
constitutional, no group libel is actionable under them unless it presents a
"clear and present danger" of causing violence. It is thus evident
that if criminal actions for group defamation can be maintained at all, they
will only be permitted under a very limited set of circumstances.

The principle set out in Beauharnais v. Illinois, supra, appeared to be
further restricted by the Supreme Court in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376
U.S. 254 (1964). In that case, the New York Times published an advertisement
setting forth information, expressing an opinion, reciting grievances and
protesting claimed abuses, and seeking financial support on behalf of the Negro
right-to-vote movement and the Negro student movement. The Commissioner of the
City of Montgomery, Alabama, brought a civil libel action against the publisher
of the newspaper. A court in Montgomery County awarded the plaintiff $500,000
in damages and the Supreme Court of Alabama upheld the decision. The United
States Supreme Court held that the rule of law applied by the Alabama courts
was constitutionally deficient as it failed to provide the safeguards for
freedom of speech that were required by the American Constitution.

The respondent relied heavily on earlier pronouncements of the Supreme Court
contained in the Beauharnais decision to the effect that the Constitution did
not protect libelous publications. Justice Brennan speaking for the court
stated that in Beauharnais the court had sustained the Illinois criminal libel
statute as it applied to a publication which was held to be both defamatory of
a racial group and "liable to cause violence and disorder". He
observed at p. 268 that the court had been careful to note that it
"retains and exercises authority to nullify action which encroaches on
freedom of utterance under the guise of punishing libel"; for ''public
men, are, as it were, public property", and "discussion cannot be
denied and the right, as well as the duty, of criticism must not be stifled".

Justice Brennan went on to state at p. 269 that the court was:

... compelled by neither precedent nor policy to
give any more weight to the epithet "libel" than to other "mere
labels" of state law ... "Like insurrection, contempt, advocacy of
unlawful acts, breach of the peace, obscenity, solicitation of legal business,
and the various other formulae for the repression of expression that have been
challenged in this Court, libel can claim no talismanic immunity from
constitutional limitations. It must be measured by standards that satisfy the
First Amendment. The general proposition that freedom of expression upon public
questions is secured by the First Amendment has long been settled by our
decisions. The constitutional safeguard, we have said, "was fashioned to assure
unfettered interchange of ideas for the bringing about of political and social
changes desired by the people" ...

Justice Brennan quoted Bridges v. California, 314 U.S. 252 (1941), to the
effect that "it is a prized American privilege to speak one's mind,
although not always with perfect good taste, on all public institutions".

Generally speaking the American authorities maintain that freedom of speech
is entitled to constitutional protection unless it is a lie, knowingly and
deliberately published, or if the statement is found to constitute a clear and
imminent danger. The American position was put forward in this way by Justice
Brandeis in Whitney v. California, 47 S.Ct. 641 (1927), at p. 648:

Fear of serious injury cannot alone justify
suppression of free speech and assembly. Men feared witches and burnt women. It
is the function of speech to free men from the bondage of irrational fears. To
justify suppression of free speech there must be reasonable ground to fear that
serious evil will result if free speech is practiced. There must be reasonable
ground to believe that the danger apprehended is imminent. There must be
reasonable ground to believe that the evil to be prevented is a serious one.

In summary it would seem that in the United States that the statements made
by the appellants would be entitled to constitutional protection unless either
the appellants had knowingly published a lie, or the statements constituted a
clear and present danger.

(c) The consideration of s. 2(b) (and s. 1) of
the
Charter
in other provinces

There are conflicting decisions in the appellate courts of other provinces
as to how
s. 2(b)
and
s. 1
of the
Charter
are to be interpreted and applied. It
may be of assistance to review the approach other appellate courts have taken,
although either side may take comfort from some of the decisions.

(i) Quebec

In Irwin Toy Ltd. v. A.-G. Que. (1986),
1986 CanLII 186 (QC CA)
, 32 D.L.R. (4th) 641, 14 C.P.R. (3d)
60, [1986] R.J.Q. 2441, the Quebec Court of Appeal had to determine whether a
section of the Province of Quebec Consumer Protection Act, S.Q. 1978, c. 9,
which prohibited commercial advertising directed at persons under 13 years of

s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
. Jacques J.A., speaking for the majority,
stated a pp. 650-1:

The purpose of the
Charter
is, among other
things, to guarantee certain rights and certain freedoms listed therein. It was
not intended as a law which would protect only what existed before it came into

have no effect.

. . . . .

The Constitution was enacted in order to change
things in the country and many things have been changed and will be changed,
gradually as time passes, as society evolves and as the
Charter
is applied.

He observed that the economic choices that citizens are required to make are
just as important as their artistic and cultural choices. He found that
commercial expression was included in freedom of expression as guaranteed by
s.
2(b)
of the
Charter
and that
s. 1
could not be applied. Thus he concluded that
the impugned provision of the Consumer Protection Act was not a limit on free

Vallerand J.A., in his minority reasons, agreed that commercial speech or
advertising came within the
s. 2
(b) guarantee of freedom of expression.
However, he was of the view that the Consumer Protection Act did constitute a

(ii) Nova Scotia

The majority of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in R. v. Skinner (1987),
1987 CanLII 133 (NS CA)
, 35
C.C.C. (3d) 203, 58 C.R. (3d) 137, 79 N.S.R. (2d) 8, considered the

(iii) British Columbia

In Re Cromer and B.C. Teachers' Federation (1986),
1986 CanLII 143 (BC CA)

[1986] 5 W.W.R. 638, 4 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273, the Court of Appeal of British
Columbia considered the constitutional validity of a provision of the

guarantee. Some portions of his reasons were quoted with approval in R. v.
Zundel (1987),
1987 CanLII 121 (ON CA)

The Charter does not purport to confer new
freedoms. It gives a constitutional guarantee to the old freedoms and, in so

1 merely places limits on the extent of the constitutional guarantee. The
freedom of expression itself remains the same freedom as existed before the
adoption of the
Charter
, and it remains subject to the same balancing process
against other important and often compelling values.

These words seem to support the concept that the rights guaranteed by the

are frozen and limited to those rights which existed at the moment of

(iv) Manitoba

In Reference re
Criminal Code, ss. 193
and 195.1(1)(c) (1987),

1987 CanLII 6801 (MB CA)
, 38 C.C.C.
(3d) 408, [1987] 6 W.W.R. 289, 49 Man. R. (2d) 1, the Court of Appeal of

.

(v) Alberta

In Re Grier and Alberta Optometric Assn. (1987),
1987 ABCA 149 (CanLII)
, 42 D.L.R. (4th) 327, [1987]
5 W.W.R. 539, 53 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289, the Alberta Court of Appeal rejected the

D.L.R., pp. 543-4 W.W.R.:

With respect, I do not agree. Indeed, I hold
precisely the opposite view. The essence of the view just quoted is that the

the "unregulated area". The "regulation" that the court has

I accept that the Ontario court placed in the

perhaps necessarily) limited by the laws in force before the

came to
be. By this view, the Charter guarantees whatever measure of freedom the

does not merely affirm existing rights. I
thought this issue had been put to rest by Chief Justice Dickson speaking for

"... it is certain that the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
does not simply "recognize and declare"
existing rights as they were circumscribed by legislation current at the time
of the Charter's entrenchment. The language of the Charter is imperative. It

(His emphasis.)

1987 ABCA 153 (CanLII)
, 36 C.C.C. (3d) 105, 43 D.L.R. (4th) 111, 58 C.R.

of the
